means: The short window after sunset or before sunrise. It usually gives a deep blue sky while city and window lights are already on, so warm and cool tones sit side by side.
Low sun shortly after sunrise or before sunset. Expect warm, soft, directional light and long shadows.
Fading evening light. It darkens the sky and brings out lamps, windows and signs without going fully to night.
First light of the day. Tends toward cool, pale tones, low contrast and empty, quiet scenes.
Puts a low, warm sun at the horizon. Often adds haze, long shadows and a gradient sky.
A low sun with strong orange and pink in the sky. Subjects in front of it tend to fall into silhouette.
Sets the scene after dark, so artificial light does the work: windows, street lamps, signs, the moon.
Warm, slanted light that is softer than midday but brighter than golden hour.
High, hard sun. Colours are bright, shadows are short and sit directly under things.
Clean, gentle light with a slightly cool cast. Reads as fresh and calm.
The thin band of light at the very edge of the day. It usually lands only on the highest parts of the scene.
Light from one side through a window. It shapes faces and objects softly and falls off into shadow on the far side.
Asks for daylight only, with no visible flash or studio lamps. The look is softer and less staged.
Diffuse light with gentle shadow edges. Flattering on faces and food, and lower in contrast.
Pushes the light toward amber. Scenes feel later in the day, lamp-lit or cosy.
Cloud cover acting as one huge soft light. Shadows nearly disappear and colours stay even.
Small warm light sources inside the scene. They make pools of glow and leave the rest darker.
Saturated coloured light from signs. It tints nearby surfaces and looks strongest on wet streets at night.
Makes something a light source in its own right, with a soft halo around it.
Living things that give off their own cool blue-green light, usually in an otherwise dark scene.
Cool, dim, single-source light. Colours go blue and shadows stay soft but deep.
Light from behind the subject. It draws a bright edge around it and separates it from the background.
Implies a low sun and adds strong lines of dark across the ground.
Visible shafts of light through haze, dust or trees. They need something in the air to show up.
Ribbons of green and violet light in a night sky, usually reflected in snow or water below.
Hides distance and lowers contrast. Shapes further away fade out, which adds depth.
A lighter veil than fog. It softens edges and catches light without hiding the scene.
Thin atmosphere that fades far objects and makes light look warmer and softer.
Adds wet, reflective surfaces and streaks in the air. Lights at night double up in puddles.
Brightens the ground, simplifies shapes and bounces light up into shadows.
Dark, heavy cloud and uneven light. Raises drama and contrast.
Soft white vapour that catches light. In food and street scenes it signals heat and freshness.
Drifting grey haze that shows light beams and adds texture to the air.
A dark, glossy ground that mirrors lights above it. A common way to get reflections in street scenes.
Asks for mirrored light on water, glass or wet ground, which adds brightness to the lower half of the frame.
The wavering air above hot ground. It softens distant detail and reads as desert or road heat.
Asks for the result to look like a photograph rather than an illustration: real lens behaviour, real materials, natural light.
Borrows the look of a film frame: wide composition, controlled colour, deliberate lighting and some depth.
Unposed and observational. People are caught mid-action and the lighting looks found, not arranged.
An unposed moment. Subjects are not looking at the camera and expressions are natural.
The polished look of a magazine spread: clean styling, careful light and a clear subject.
Everyday scenes shot to look relaxed and appealing, with warm light and tidy surroundings.
Public places and passers-by, shot as found. Usually wide enough to show the surroundings.
Close, appetising framing of a dish with soft side light and shallow focus.
A long-lens look: the animal sharp, the background blurred, natural behaviour.
Landscapes and plants shot realistically, with natural colour and light.
Buildings with straight verticals, clean lines and even light, so the structure itself is the subject.
The car, train or craft as hero: low viewpoint, clean reflections, uncluttered background.
Close portraits with soft, even light and attention to skin, hair and eyes.
Objects arranged on purpose and lit carefully, with nothing moving.
A controlled indoor setup: plain background, deliberate lights, no stray detail.
The look of design paintings made for films and games: painterly, atmospheric, built to sell an idea of a place.
Visible brushwork and painted light instead of photographic detail.
A drawn or painted picture, not a photo. Shapes are cleaner and colour is more deliberate.
Painted or rendered views of planets, moons and deep sky, usually with strong scale contrast.
Japanese animation style: clean line work, flat colour areas, expressive eyes and simplified shading.
Colour in flat steps with hard edges between light and shadow, as in hand-painted animation frames.
Printed comic style: inked outlines, bold flat colour and dynamic poses.
The dot pattern of old colour printing. It makes an image read as a printed comic page.
Heavy black contour lines around shapes, which flatten the image and make it graphic.
Science-fiction design language: advanced machines, clean or industrial surfaces, artificial light.
Dense future city at night: neon, rain, cables and screens, with high contrast between glow and shadow.
Dark, high-contrast and moody, with hard shadows and little colour.
An older photographic look: faded colour, softer detail, period objects.
Soft edges and visible strokes, as if made with a brush.
Pale, low-saturation colours. The mood turns gentle and light.
Removes colour so shape, light and texture carry the picture.
Deep blacks and bright highlights with little in between. Punchier and more dramatic.
Stronger light and shadow, bigger skies, more tension. A general push away from a flat, neutral look.
Pushes scale: vast spaces, tiny figures, towering forms.
Calms the scene: fewer people, stiller air, softer light.
Pulls the camera back to show the whole scene. The subject gets smaller and the setting matters more.
An even broader view than wide, emphasising how far the scene stretches.
A very wide, level view across a landscape or city, often from a distance.
Looks down from the air. Patterns and layout show up; individual people do not.
Camera pointing straight down. Common for food and tabletop scenes.
A raised viewpoint, such as a rooftop or hillside, looking across the scene instead of up at it.
Camera at standing height on the ground, inside the scene.
Camera near the ground looking up. Subjects look taller and more powerful.
Fills the frame with the subject and drops most of the background.
Extreme close range on something small, with a very thin slice in focus.
Frames one person or animal as the subject, usually head and shoulders with a soft background.
Only a thin slice is sharp. The background melts away and attention goes to the subject.
Out-of-focus lights turned into soft discs behind the subject.
Streaks on moving things. It shows speed while still parts stay sharp.
Moving lights drawn out into lines, as in a long exposure of traffic at night.
A slow shutter. Anything that moves, water, clouds, traffic, stars, smooths into soft streaks while still things stay sharp.
The subject as a dark shape against a brighter background. Outline matters; inner detail goes.
Puts something close to the lens, which adds depth in front of the main subject.
Keeps something small and far away. Often used to stop people or landmarks taking over the frame.
The outline of a city's buildings seen from outside it. Sets the view far enough back to read the whole shape.
The dense centre of a city: tall buildings, lit windows, busy streets.
A city or town edge on water, which brings reflections and an open foreground.
A slow, smooth glide of the camera. Enough movement to feel alive without pans, zooms or shake.
Holds the camera still so only things inside the scene move.
The camera moves slowly toward the subject, tightening attention on it.
The camera circles the subject, showing it from changing sides. It works best on one object with open space round it.
Tells the model to keep motion unhurried. Fast movement is where video models most often break.
Small repeating movement on water or cloth. An easy, believable motion for a short clip.
Light that wavers in brightness: lanterns, neon, screens. It gives a still scene a small, constant change, which helps a clip read as video.
Slow, floating movement. Of the camera, a smooth glide in one direction. Of things in the scene, fog, steam or clouds moving gently. Either way it adds life without changing the layout.
A slow side-to-side movement of something hanging or rooted, such as lanterns, grass or branches. A gentle motion that video models tend to keep stable.
Asks the model to leave out lettering, which it often renders as gibberish.
Asks for a clean frame with no stamp or signature in the corners.
Keeps people small, turned away or soft, so nobody is identifiable.
Empties the scene of figures, so the place itself is the subject.
States that everyone shown is an adult.
Rules out one viewpoint, which pushes the model toward the other one named in the prompt.
Asks for a new design instead of an existing character or brand.
